routes.description: Establish physical resurrection through a cumulative inference from bodily appearance testimony, the empty tomb, sincere proclamation, conversions, and relevant miracle evidence.
routes.successCriteria: The combined evidence must support physical resurrection as a more adequate explanation than visionary, legendary, relocation, theft, or insincerity hypotheses.

motionBridge.description: The cumulative historical evidence must make Jesus's physical resurrection historically reasonable.

centralBridges.description: The reported individual and group appearances must concern the same Jesus alive in an embodied state after death.
Jesus must have received an identifiable burial followed by a genuinely missing body.
Resurrection must jointly explain the early bodily proclamation, sincere experiences, conversions, and tomb evidence.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Apostolic danger and transformation must support the sincerity of witnesses positioned to know what they proclaimed.
Rival and later miracle reports must be assessed by evidential differences without excluding supernatural events categorically.

routes.description: Withhold the physical-resurrection conclusion by showing that the testimony is ambiguous, rival religious evidence is comparable, and ordinary alternatives remain available.
routes.successCriteria: The record must remain insufficient to establish firsthand bodily encounters or to prefer resurrection over visionary experience, narrative development, relocation, or theft.

motionBridge.description: The surviving historical record must underdetermine whether Jesus physically rose from the dead.

centralBridges.description: The earliest and surviving appearance sources must fail to establish secure firsthand testimony to a physically risen body.
Comparable religious testimony and costly commitment must limit the discriminating force of Christian witness claims.
Visionary appearances and non-resurrection explanations of an empty tomb must remain historically available.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Persecution evidence must be tied specifically to eyewitness knowledge of bodily resurrection before supporting that conclusion.
Apologetic features and differences among later narratives must constrain their use as independent historical corroboration.

sectionSelections.title: Appearance Testimony and Physicality
sectionSelections.rationale: The motion requires more than survival or vision, making the evidential character and bodily interpretation of the reported appearances indispensable.

proSelections.proposition: Reported individual and group encounters provide historical grounds for concluding that Jesus was alive after his death.
Paul taught embodied resurrection, and the physical features attributed to Jesus's appearances distinguish them from acknowledged visions.

conSelections.proposition: Comparable experiences occur outside Christianity, while the sources remain unclear about whether Jesus's risen body was physical.
Paul is unclear about physical resurrection, while later Gospel appearance accounts become more elaborate and theological.

sectionSelections.title: Rival Miracles and Witness Comparisons
sectionSelections.rationale: The treatment of comparable religious claims determines whether Christian testimony has distinctive force or depends on inconsistent evidential standards.

proSelections.proposition: Well-attested Marian apparitions raise the probability of resurrection because they fit Christian theology more readily if the resurrection occurred.
Mormon witness claims are weaker analogues because incentives, expectations, source discrepancies, and contrary evidence reduce their credibility.

conSelections.proposition: Mormon witness and transfiguration traditions are comparable to early Christian testimony and expose the limited verifiability of Paul's group report.
Persecution and growth do not distinguish Christianity from Mormonism, and evidence that apostles died for resurrection belief is sparse.

sectionSelections.title: Sincerity, Conversion, and Martyrdom
sectionSelections.rationale: Transformations and costly commitment bear on witness sincerity, but their relevance depends on access to and suffering for the specific bodily claim.

proSelections.proposition: Apostolic danger supports the sincerity of informed witnesses, while Paul's conversion supplies an explanatory feature absent from the Mormon parallel.
Resurrection explains the conversions of prior unbelievers and persecutors and the apostles' transformation into bold proclaimers.

conSelections.proposition: Persecution and martyrdom do not establish eyewitness knowledge of bodily resurrection when the clearest cases involve visions or unspecified beliefs.
A strong historical case would require firsthand bodily-appearance testimony and persecution specifically for that belief, which the surviving record lacks.

sectionSelections.title: Burial and the Empty Tomb
sectionSelections.rationale: A missing body in an identifiable tomb is a principal bridge from appearance belief to physical resurrection and a focal point for ordinary alternatives.

proSelections.proposition: Matthew's dispute over a stolen body may preserve evidence that Jesus's body was genuinely missing despite the narrative's apologetic purpose.
Specific non-resurrection hypotheses lose probability when combined, and grave robbery poorly fits the retained burial goods and known practices.

conSelections.proposition: Women discovering the tomb is narratively expected rather than embarrassing, while conflicting sequences weaken that authenticity inference.
If an empty tomb existed, temporary emergency burial followed by relocation or theft could explain it without resurrection.

sectionSelections.title: Cumulative Inference and Supernatural Possibility
sectionSelections.rationale: The ultimate historical conclusion depends on whether the combined evidence favors resurrection and whether supernatural explanations remain eligible for comparison.

proSelections.proposition: Early bodily proclamation, sincere individual and group experiences, Paul's conversion, and a checkable tomb are cumulatively explained by resurrection.
Better-documented later Christian miracle reports make universal dismissal of supernatural claims less probable and challenge strict naturalism.

conSelections.proposition: Evidence for Jesus before crucifixion is stronger than evidence for postmortem appearances because the latter lacks independent extra-Christian corroboration.
Visionary appearances may be genuine experiences without establishing that Jesus appeared in a physically resurrected body.
